content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler Juice, Mixed Fruit is a 100 % natural fruit juice specially formulated for children from 1 year old. It blends apple, pear, banana and berries, without added sugar or preservatives.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The juice is made from carefully selected fruits grown without pesticides.
Each bottle contains about 120 ml, an ideal portion size for toddlers.
It provides approximately 15 mg of vitamin C to support immunity.
The product meets strict quality standards and complies with Russian GOST for baby foods.
Packaging is made from safe PET material that is recyclable.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamin C from the fruit blend helps protect the body against common colds.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Natural fruit sugars give a quick source of energy needed by active toddlers.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: A modest amount of fiber aids regular digestion.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: The juice supplies vitamins A, B6 and folate, important for growth and development.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The liquid content helps maintain proper hydration in young children.

items.title: Fruit allergy
items.content: Children with known allergies to apples, pears or berries should consult a pediatrician before consumption.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although no sugar is added, natural fruit sugars may affect blood glucose levels in diabetic children.

items.title: Not suitable for infants under 1 year
items.content: The juice can pose a choking risk and stress the kidneys of infants.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the juice chilled in small portions (30–60 ml) after meals. Do not keep opened juice at room temperature for more than 24 hours.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bottle in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep it refrigerated and consume within 2‑3 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Bagel, whole grain white is a baked product made from whole‑grain wheat flour, prepared using the traditional method of boiling the dough before baking. It has a dense, slightly chewy texture, a golden crust, and a soft, mildly sweet crumb.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bagels originated in Eastern European Jewish communities in the 19th century.
The classic preparation involves briefly boiling the dough in water with a touch of soda or honey, giving the crust its characteristic shine.
The whole‑grain version retains bran and germ, increasing fiber and micronutrient content.
Bagels are commonly served with cream cheese, smoked salmon, avocado, or simply with butter.
In the United States more than 1.5 billion bagels are sold each year.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain flour provides a high amount of soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Bagels supply thiamine, niacin, and folate, which aid energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Boiling the dough and the whole‑grain structure slow carbohydrate absorption, helping to maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving delivers about 9 g of protein, useful for muscle repair.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: Bagels contain iron, magnesium, and zinc, essential for blood formation and immune health.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Bagels are made from wheat and are unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Because of their dense structure, bagels are relatively high in calories; portion control is advised for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Traditional recipes contain salt; individuals with hypertension should choose low‑salt versions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the bagel in half and toast it, then spread with cream cheese, hummus, avocado, or top with smoked salmon. It also works well as a sandwich base with vegetables, turkey, or egg.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the bagel in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze it in a freezer‑safe bag – it stays fresh for up to 3 months. Reheat in a toaster or oven before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Red cabbage (Brassica oleracea) retains its vivid color and tender texture after cooking. It belongs to the cruciferous family and is rich in vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants. Cooked red cabbage is commonly used in side dishes, salads, and soups.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Red cabbage contains anthocyanins – natural pigments that give it a deep purple hue.
In ancient cultures cabbage was used to aid digestion and symbolized prosperity.
Cabbage can accumulate heavy metals from soil, so sourcing from reputable farms is important.
Cooking cabbage in a small amount of water helps preserve most of its nutrients.
Red cabbage is a staple in many Eastern European dishes, such as sauerkraut.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Cooked red cabbage retains a substantial amount of vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and supports a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Anthocyanins and other polyphenols protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Cabbage provides potassium, magnesium, and iron, which are vital for normal bodily functions.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Cruciferous vegetables can cause increased gas production in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Interaction with anticoagulants
items.content: High vitamin K intake may affect the efficacy of blood‑thinning medications.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Improperly washed cabbage may retain pesticide residues; thorough rinsing before cooking is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked red cabbage can be served as a standalone side, added to salads, stews, soups, or used as a filling for pies. For a caramelized flavor, briefly sauté it after boiling.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked cabbage in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags to retain flavor and nutrients.

content.title: About
content.content: Cheese spread in a pressurized can is an aerosol product packaged under pressure, allowing easy spraying of a smooth cheese cream. It typically contains cream cheese, vegetable oils, flavorings, and preservatives, providing a creamy texture and long shelf life.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The product is sold in aerosol cans, which simplifies portion control and saves time.
Cheese spread is often used in sandwiches, snacks, and sauces.
Pressure inside the can keeps the spread soft even at low temperatures.
Variants may include additives such as garlic, herbs, or spices for flavor variety.
Cans are usually made of aluminum, protecting the product from light and oxygen.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: The cream cheese component provides calcium, essential for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Cheese spread offers a modest amount of protein that supports tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The product may contain vitamins B2 and B12, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Contains dairy ingredients that can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Cheese spread often contains saturated and trans fats, so it should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some versions include artificial preservatives, which may not be suitable for those avoiding additives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Spray the spread onto bread, crackers, vegetable sticks, or use as a base for sauces and dips. It can also be added to hot dishes at the end of cooking for a creamy finish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the can in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, use within 1‑2 weeks. Discard if the smell or taste changes.

content.title: About
content.content: Pasta, vegetable, cooked is a ready‑to‑eat product consisting of boiled pasta mixed with vegetable ingredients (such as carrots, broccoli, tomatoes) and often seasoned with herbs and spices. It is convenient for quick meals and can be served as a main dish or a side.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Vegetable pasta is often made from whole‑grain flour, increasing its nutritional value.
A variety of vegetables can be included, making the dish richer in vitamins and minerals.
These ready‑made mixes are widely used in school cafeterias and office canteens to save time.
The pasta can be fortified with extra plant proteins like soy or pea protein.
There are many regional versions, e.g., Italian pasta with tomato‑vegetable sauce or Asian noodles with vegetable stir‑fry.

items.title: Rich source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Pasta provides sustained energy and a feeling of fullness thanks to the slow release of glucose.

items.title: Contains vegetables
items.content: The vegetable component adds vitamins (A, C, K) and minerals (potassium, magnesium) as well as antioxidants.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: When combined with legumes or soy, the dish becomes a good source of plant‑based protein.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from whole‑grain pasta and vegetables promotes healthy bowel function.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with many meat‑based meals, vegetable pasta typically contains little saturated fat.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: Traditional wheat pasta contains gluten, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Salt and additives
items.content: Prepared mixes may have high sodium levels and food additives, so check the label.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Some recipes include nuts, soy, or dairy, which are common allergens.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: While moderate in calories, large portions can contribute to weight gain.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the pasta in the microwave or on the stove, add fresh herbs, cheese, olive oil, or a protein‑rich sauce. It works well as a standalone meal, a side to meat or fish, and can be tossed into salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked vegetable pasta in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C in an airtight container for up to 3–4 days. For longer keeping, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Discard if it develops off‑odors or an unusual appearance.

content.title: About
content.content: Cheese French fries are a fast‑food dish consisting of deep‑fried potato sticks topped with melted cheese. They are commonly served in fast‑food restaurants as a hot snack or side.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: French fries originated in the United States in the early 20th century and quickly spread worldwide.
The cheese used is often processed cheese that melts smoothly when heated.
In many countries the fries are offered with a variety of sauces such as ketchup, mayo, cheese sauce, or garlic aioli.
A popular variant uses shredded cheddar that forms a crispy crust after baking.
The dish is typically served in disposable cardboard containers for on‑the‑go eating.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Potatoes are rich in carbohydrates that provide quick energy.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Potatoes contain vitamin B6 and niacin, important for metabolism.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: Potatoes are a good source of potassium, which supports heart and muscle function.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus from cheese
items.content: The cheese adds calcium and phosphorus, essential for bone health.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Cheese contributes a modest amount of dairy protein.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Frying and cheese make the dish calorie‑dense, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Both the oil used for frying and the cheese contain saturated fats, which can raise cholesterol when consumed in excess.

items.title: Salt
items.content: The dish is often heavily salted, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to casein or lactose found in cheese.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cheese French fries are served hot, straight from the fryer. They can be eaten with the hands, using the container or a paper tray, and are often accompanied by dipping sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The dish is best enjoyed immediately. Leftovers can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 1‑2 days and reheated in an oven to restore crispness.
